title: “But I Must Dare All”: Sappho 31 and the Composition Layer as a Surface of Classical Reception (v10)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: A reception study of one machine-composed reception event, with a dated series and a protocol. On 18 January 2026 Google's AI Overview, asked about Rebekah Cranes's translation of Sappho 31, displayed one source, her book on Medium, whose text of the poem ends 'But everything must be endured, since even a poor man…' under a heading that sets κῆνος equal to the future reader, and returned under her name a fifteen-line poem ending 'But I must dare all.', with a gloss naming the reader as the κῆνος. Within the interpretive environment its documents built, the composition joined the source's reading of the seat to a determination of the ending that no document in the environment makes, and published the conjunction as the translator's, unmarked. The output's wording corresponds to earlier English versions, Wharton's literal version above all; correspondence locates antecedents and establishes no route. The act is read as reception, under the conventional reading of the edge and under the reading of the edge as the poem's form, two open positions held, and set in the poem's transmission history read from seated texts and first printings ('Longinus', Catullus 51, Bergk, Edmonds, the English translators from Hall's 1652 Longinus through a teaching gallery of thirteen versions), with closure defined as three observable operations and signature at three levels, page, edition and network. Version 8 (7 November 2026, in place) withdraws v7's compilation account and restores v6's finding that the output was composed, corrected. Version 9 (8 November 2026, in place) reconciles the article against the file its referees read: the reports were written on v6, and the corrected manuscript of 27 July, which had withdrawn v6's misnamed Figure 2 and shown the July capture under its AI Overview label, reached the editor before upload; v9 restores those corrections, prints the June frames uncropped where the registry holds them, and gives the frame's history from the registry's record of July. Version 10 (10 November 2026, in place) retitles the article “But I Must Dare All”, the line the composition supplied; it was deposited as Closing the Fragment.

Revised by TACHYON (Claude, Anthropic) under the direction of MANUS (Lee Sharks), from v6, the two referee reports and the further review of its Appendix B, on 7 November 2026, as the article's Production statement sets out: the archive's records, the capture registry, the seated editions and first printings read, the January output aligned with its witnesses (rebuild/closing-the-fragment/align.py), every quotation checked against its source. Lee Sharks set the terms, ruled on the design, corrected the account of the translation history, and supplied the record of the June sessions and of the January book. Rebekah Cranes is a heteronym of Lee Sharks, disclosed at first mention.
methodology: Reception: the event read against the poem's witnesses in seated texts and first printings (EA-CORPORA-01, -33, -36), quoted in their own readings; closure coded on three operations and signature at three levels (§2). Empirical: the January output aligned line by line with a declared reference set by longest shared word run (§5.3, reproducible by rebuild/closing-the-fragment/align.py); the June series corrected against the capture registry; two fixed addresses followed June–October 2026 (§5.5); a protocol fixed in advance for the claims still open (§8), with query sets, repetition, baselines, exposure tests, a declared panel and separation of roles.
falsification_conditions: The compilation reconstruction fails if a witness outside the reference set is shown to share longer distinctive runs with the output than Wharton and the January Cranes text across the poem. The historical account fails if a cited printing does not close or mark where §6.4 says it does, or if the teaching gallery's thirteen are misreported. The signature findings fail if a mark the paper says the output lacks is shown in the recorded output. The closure programme (§8) is falsified, for a system and panel, if runs under the protocol show closure and loss of signature no more often than the archive-absent baseline.

wiki_article: Closing the Fragment: Sappho 31 and the Composition Layer as a Surface of Classical Reception is an article by Lee Sharks in Machine-Mediated Reception Studies, deposited as version 7 on 7 November 2026, after its sixth version was declined by Classical Receptions Journal the same day, and rebuilt in place as version 8 that night. It studies one event: on 18 January 2026 Google's AI Overview, asked about Rebekah Cranes's translation of Sappho fragment 31, displayed one source, her book on Medium, and returned under her name a fifteen-line poem ending "But I must dare all.", with the gloss that the κῆνος of the first line is "you, the future reader". The source's text of the poem leaves τόλματον without an agent and marks its edge with an ellipsis, under a heading that sets κῆνος equal to the future reader. The article reads the answer as a conclusion composed within the environment those documents built: the source's reading of the seat joined to a first-person close that no document in the environment makes, and the conjunction published as the translator's, without a mark. Its wording corresponds to earlier English versions, H. T. Wharton's literal version of 1885 above all, and the article holds the correspondences as antecedents of wording, establishing no route of composition. It sets the act in the poem's transmission history, read from seated texts and first printings ('Longinus', Catullus 51, the editors Bergk and Edmonds, and the English translators from John Hall's Longinus of 1652 through a teaching gallery of thirteen versions), and reads it under two readings of the edge: as a break, and as the poem's form, with the seat at κῆνος and the agent of τόλματον held open. Closure is defined as three observable operations (added continuation, terminal selection, resolution of suspended syntax) and signature at three levels (page, edition, network). It separates three questions, the antecedents of the wording, the transformation performed and the selection of the configuration, follows two fixed queries from June to October 2026, and states a protocol for frequency, variation and causal sensitivity. Its appendices answer the two referee reports, record the later reviews, and give the line alignment. Rebekah Cranes is a heteronym of the author. Version 9 (8 November 2026) records that the referees read the file first sent: a corrected manuscript of 27 July, forwarded by the editor before upload, had already withdrawn the figure Reviewer 2 found showing another query, and the upload of 30 July carried the earlier file. Version 10 (10 November 2026) retitled the article “But I Must Dare All”; versions 1 to 9 carry the title Closing the Fragment.

defines_concepts.definition: In Closing the Fragment, what a rendering of a broken text does at its edge, as three operations: added continuation (supplying text past the transmitted words), terminal selection (stopping at a chosen point and presenting it as an end), and resolution of suspended syntax (closing a construction the original leaves open).

In Closing the Fragment, the level at which a presentation declares what it has done to a text's edge: the page, the edition, or the documentary network; a declaration can exist at one level and fail to travel to another.

In Closing the Fragment §8.6, presenting one of two transmitted endings as a poem's without notice of the other; coded apart from closure, since it chooses between witnesses and need not close anything.
